::: {.oneline}
A photon is one quantum of energy in a single mode of the electromagnetic
field — a property of the field, not an object travelling through it.
:::

## Short answer

Quantising the free electromagnetic field turns each mode $(\mathbf k, \lambda)$
into an independent harmonic oscillator with frequency $\omega_{\mathbf k}$. A
photon is one step up the ladder of one such oscillator:

$$
\hat H = \sum_{\mathbf k \lambda} \hbar\omega_{\mathbf k}
\left( \hat a^\dagger_{\mathbf k \lambda}\hat a_{\mathbf k \lambda}
+ \tfrac{1}{2} \right)
$$ {#eq-field-h}

The state $\hat a^\dagger_{\mathbf k\lambda}\lvert 0\rangle$ has one more
quantum in that mode. That is all "a photon" means. It carries energy
$\hbar\omega_{\mathbf k}$, momentum $\hbar\mathbf k$ and polarisation $\lambda$,
but it has no position operator and no trajectory. A mode extends over the
whole quantisation volume, so a single photon is not localised anywhere in
particular.

The word gets used for a second thing: the click in a detector. That click is
an absorption event in the detector's matter, and it is discrete because the
*atoms* have discrete levels. The two meanings coincide often enough that they
get conflated, and occasionally they come apart.

## Why it is set up this way

Nothing forces the ladder interpretation — it falls out of imposing canonical
commutation relations on the vector potential. The physics that demands it is
the observation that field energy exchange with matter is quantised in units of
$\hbar\omega$, which is what makes @eq-field-h more than bookkeeping.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation: from Maxwell to oscillators

In Coulomb gauge, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf A = 0$, the free field is transverse.
Expand in plane-wave modes in a volume $V$:

$$
\mathbf A(\mathbf r,t) = \sum_{\mathbf k\lambda}
\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2\varepsilon_0 \omega_{\mathbf k} V}}
\left[
a_{\mathbf k\lambda}\,\boldsymbol\epsilon_{\mathbf k\lambda} e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}
+ \mathrm{c.c.}
\right]
$$

Substituting into the field energy
$H = \frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int d^3r\,(E^2 + c^2 B^2)$ and using the
transversality condition, the cross terms between different modes integrate to
zero and

$$
H = \sum_{\mathbf k\lambda} \hbar\omega_{\mathbf k}
\,|a_{\mathbf k\lambda}|^2 .
$$

Each mode is a decoupled harmonic oscillator. Promoting
$a_{\mathbf k\lambda} \to \hat a_{\mathbf k\lambda}$ with
$[\hat a_{\mathbf k\lambda}, \hat a^\dagger_{\mathbf k'\lambda'}]
= \delta_{\mathbf k\mathbf k'}\delta_{\lambda\lambda'}$
gives @eq-field-h, zero-point term included.

The choice of plane waves is convenience. Any complete set of solutions to the
free wave equation defines modes, and therefore defines what "one photon"
means. Photon number is basis-dependent in exactly this sense.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Aside: why there is no photon wavefunction

A position operator would require localising the field arbitrarily sharply,
which costs unbounded energy and mixes positive- and negative-frequency parts
of the field. The closest useful object is the photon-detection amplitude,
which is what a photodetector's response is proportional to, and which is a
statement about the *field at the detector*, not about where a particle was.
:::

## Common confusions

- **"A photon is a small packet of light travelling from source to detector."**
  Modes are delocalised. Localisation in an experiment comes from the geometry
  of the source and the detector, not from the photon.
- **"A laser emits photons one at a time."** A laser emits a coherent state,
  which is a superposition of *all* photon numbers with Poissonian weights. See
  [Why does a classical field require coherence?](../classical-field-coherence/index.qmd).
- **"Photon number is an absolute property of the field."** It depends on the
  mode basis, and for accelerated observers even on the observer.
